title: An Interpretable Deep Learning Framework for Evaluating Sensor Networks in Urban Drainage Systems
content:
Abstract

Reliable monitoring of urban drainage systems (UDS) depends on how effectively sensors capture and propagate hydrodynamic conditions across the network. Existing studies have mainly treated sensor networks as a pre-deployment placement problem, whereas the post-deployment diagnosis of sensor contribution, redundancy, and spatial representativeness remains insufficiently addressed. This study proposes an interpretable post-deployment diagnostic framework for evaluating sensor networks in UDS. The framework first reconstructs system-wide water-level states from sparse observations and then learns directional dependency structures among monitoring nodes. Based on the learned dependency structures, three interpretable indicators–effective number, top mass, and coverage radius–are introduced to characterize the breadth, concentration, and spatial reach of sensor influence. Results show that the framework achieves high reconstruction accuracy under sparse monitoring conditions, with a mean Nash-Sutcliffe efficiency exceeding 0.85. The derived interpretable results remain stable across varying hydrological conditions, and the inferred node influence rankings exhibit moderate consistency with perturbation-based method, yielding Spearman’s correlation coefficients between 0.60 and 0.75. The spatial patterns of the three interpretable indicators align closely with the drainage network topology, enabling the diagnosis of distinct sensing roles, redundant information, and weakly represented areas within existing monitoring networks. The main advancement of the proposed framework is that it moves beyond ranking candidate sensor locations and instead interprets how sensors contribute to network-wide monitoring after implementation. Overall, the proposed approach provides an interpretable diagnostic basis for assessing existing sensor networks and supporting incremental improvement of monitoring strategies in urban drainage environments.
